title: Work as a function of protocol duration for the efficient erasure of an underdamped memory: isothermal to adiabatic transition
authors: Nicolas Barros, Stephen Whitelam, Sergio Ciliberto, Ludovic Bellon
abstract: We use evolutionary reinforcement learning to determine efficient time-dependent erasure protocols for an underdamped cantilever moving in a double-well potential, an experimental realization of a 1-bit memory. We investigate how the mean work $\langle W \rangle $ needed to erase a bit scales as a function of the protocol duration $τ$. We find two regimes, depending on how $τ$ compares to the relaxation time of the system $t_r$. For $τ\gg t_r$, the quasistatic isothermal regime, we recover Landauer's bound plus an overhead that scales as $1/τ$, similar to the overdamped case. By contrast, for $τ<t_r$ erasure becomes adiabatic and $\langle W \rangle$ grows more slowly than in the isothermal case. This growth is bounded from below as $1/τ$, which we derive using a gedanken optimal protocol. Finally, comparison with overdamped erasure shows that learned protocols can outperform protocols that are optimal subject to equilibrium boundary conditions.
summary: This paper investigates the minimum work needed to erase a bit stored in an underdamped mechanical memory by optimizing control protocols using reinforcement learning. It reveals distinct scaling laws depending on whether the erasure process is slow (isothermal) or fast (adiabatic). The findings demonstrate that optimized, non-equilibrium protocols can achieve efficiencies surpassing those predicted by protocols constrained by equilibrium boundary conditions.
main_problem: The study determines the minimum work required to efficiently erase a bit of information stored in an underdamped memory and analyzes how this work scales with the protocol duration ($\tau$).
main_result: The work required exhibits distinct scaling regimes: quasi-static ($\tau \gg t_r$) approaches Landauer's bound plus a $1/\tau$ overhead, while fast erasures ($\tau \le t_r$) enter an adiabatic regime where learned protocols outperform equilibrium-based optimal protocols.
method: The research employs evolutionary reinforcement learning (neuroevolution) to optimize time-dependent control protocols, complemented by theoretical derivations of lower bounds using *gedanken* optimal protocols.
model_or_system: The physical system is an underdamped cantilever moving in a double-well potential, serving as an experimental model for a 1-bit memory. The dynamics are governed by the Langevin equation.
key_observables: Mean work ($\langle W \rangle$), failure probability ($P_f$), and the system's total energy ($\langle E_{tot} \rangle$).
important_parameters: Protocol duration ($\tau$), system relaxation time ($t_r$), and the ratio $\tau_r/\tau$ defining the transition between isothermal and adiabatic regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes control is limited to modulating two parameters ($z_0(t), z_1(t)$) and compares results against theoretical lower bounds derived from idealized protocols.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of mean work and failure rates for basic, learned, and optimal protocols across varying time scales ($\tau_r/\tau$), highlighting the performance gap for fast erasures.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical model and the goal (minimum work), detailing the use of reinforcement learning for protocol optimization, analyzing the scaling laws across different time regimes (isothermal vs. adiabatic), and finally comparing learned results against theoretical lower bounds.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics and information erasure bounds in a mesoscopic mechanical system, providing experimental validation of theoretical scaling laws in the transition between slow and fast driving regimes.
